source_evidence.quote: We found a positive correlation between adiponectin and total cholesterol (r = 0.27, P = 0.055), LDL (r = 0.34, P = 0.026) and SD-LDL (r = 0.41, P = 0.006) in patients with at least 3 components of MetS criteria.
Significant interaction was observed between adiponectin and metabolic syndrome in relation to serum lipid profile.
Adiponectin levels were negatively associated with waist circumference, waist-hip ratio, PTX-3 and LDL.

In 180 individuals, including controls and patients with MetS, we measured fasting plasma insulin, high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), pentraxin-3 (PTX-3), interleukin-33 (IL-33), irisin, RBP-4, and adiponectin using ELISA kits.

verdict.label: apparent_contradiction
verdict.rationale: Both claims are verified against their sources. A reports a positive correlation between serum adiponectin and SD-LDL (r = 0.41, P = 0.006) in type-2 DM patients with at least 3 MetS components, consistent with its positive adiponectin–LDL correlation (r = 0.30, P = 0.001) in the full cohort. B reports adiponectin levels negatively associated with LDL in a correlation analysis. The directions are genuinely opposite for a similar adiponectin–(SD)LDL association. A concrete contextual difference is text-supported: A's cohort consists entirely of patients with type-2 DM (173 patients, sentence 5) and A reports a significant interaction between adiponectin and metabolic syndrome in relation to lipid profile (sentence 13), whereas B's cohort is 180 individuals including non-MetS controls and patients with MetS, with no reported type-2 DM (sentence 2). This population/MetS-status difference could explain the opposing directions, so the pair is an apparent contradiction rather than a strict contradiction.
